claims.text: Sub-surface enrichment of high-surface-energy elements stabilizes HEA nanoparticle surfaces.
Sub-surface enrichment stabilizes the surface by increasing local atomic coordination energy.
Sub-surface enrichment of high-surface-energy elements delays premelting and complete melting relative to a homogeneous elemental distribution.
CrMnFeCoNi or similar HEA nanoparticles can have an FCC structure and an initially homogeneous elemental distribution.
Two nanoparticle sets will be designed, one with induced sub-surface enrichment and one with a uniform elemental distribution.
Particle size, shape, and synthesis conditions will be held constant while sub-surface composition is varied.
High-surface-energy elements such as Ru in sub-surface layers increase the dissolution potential of surface atoms.
Sub-surface Ru can stabilize Pt atoms and produce a passivating Pd or Pt shell.
High-surface-energy elements stabilize the coordination of surface atoms.
The proposed sub-surface enrichment delays surface-atom mobility.
Delayed surface-atom mobility postpones the premelting transition.
Combined ML dissolution and ML-potential melting studies predict delayed premelting from sub-surface enrichment.
Enriched nanoparticles will have a higher premelting-onset temperature than homogeneous baseline nanoparticles.
Enriched nanoparticles will have a higher complete-melting temperature than homogeneous baseline nanoparticles.
The thermal-stabilization effect should occur across the typical HEA nanoparticle compositional range used for catalysis, sensing, and related applications.
The hypothesis should hold for HEA nanoparticles with similar FCC structures and standard application-relevant compositions.
Drastic changes in particle size, shape, or crystal structure may cause other effects to dominate melting behavior.
The quantitative melting-temperature shift and minimum enrichment required for stabilization are unknown.
